newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open mostly weaker in quiet trade.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open mostly weaker in quiet trade.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened mostly softer in quiet trade on Thursday, as weakness in Canadian and U.S. bond markets was partly offset by technical shortages of T-bills in some parts of the curve, dealers said.

"There's been some fairly good profit taking overseas in the short end," said Walter Posiewko, a money market trader with Royal Bank Investment Management Inc. "I think it's just a realization by everyone that things have gone a little bit too far in a fairly short period of time."
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.04 percent from 3.01 percent at Wednesday's close.

Canadian T-bills had rallied since Tuesday when the U.S. Federal Reserve decided to hold U.S. interest rates steady. The Canadian money market benefited from speculation the Bank of Canada would not hike rates in the near future.
While T-bills weakened this morning along with softer Canadian and U.S. bond markets, Posiewko said losses were being limited by technical factors.

"There's some real technical shortages out there, some real problems. That's why there continues to be a bid in this market," said Posiewko. "It really is a very disjointed market after the events of this week."
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.36 percent from 3.34 percent. The one-year T-bill softened to yield 3.73 percent from 3.71 percent at Wednesday's close.
The call loan rate traded at 3.10 percent, the center of the Bank of Canada's 2.75-3.25 percent target range.
